interviewQuestions.question: Why might a mobile app need a different API shape than a web dashboard consuming the same underlying data?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Three real constraints a web dashboard mostly doesn't share to the same degree. First, bandwidth is metered and variable — a payload that's negligible on broadband is real latency and real data cost on cellular, and connection quality itself fluctuates moment to moment as the user moves. Second, battery: every network request wakes the device's radio, which has a real fixed cost, so five small chatty requests can cost more battery than one larger consolidated one at the same total bytes — request count matters, not just payload size. Third, and often underweighted: mobile clients can't be force-updated the way a web page refreshes to the latest JS on load, so a meaningful percentage of users are always running an older app version, and the API has to keep serving them correctly.

These three constraints directly motivate the mobile-specific practices: payload shaping (send only what a screen renders, not a generic full-resource dump), aggregation via a BFF (collapse a screen's data need into fewer round trips), cursor-based pagination (stable against list changes, unlike offset pagination), and disciplined API versioning (additive changes only, real deprecation windows informed by adoption telemetry).

I'd frame the answer around the constraints causing the practices, not just list the practices — that's what actually demonstrates understanding versus memorized best practices.

**Testing:** whether you can connect mobile-specific practices back to the actual constraints driving them.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: Design the API and BFF layer for a mobile app's home feed screen that needs the user's profile summary, a personalized content feed, and any active promotional banners — each currently served by a separate backend microservice.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd put a mobile BFF in front of the three services, so the client makes exactly one request for this screen and the BFF handles the fan-out to Profile, Feed, and Promotions services internally, in parallel where the calls don't depend on each other, then assembles one response shaped specifically for this screen — not three separate generic resource shapes stitched together client-side.

The feed portion needs pagination — cursor-based, since offset pagination would visibly skip or duplicate items if new content is inserted between the user's page requests, which is common for a content feed. I'd have the BFF return an opaque `nextCursor` and a `hasMore` flag rather than exposing anything about how the underlying feed service internally tracks position, so that internal representation can change without becoming a client-facing breaking change.

For the profile summary and promotional banners specifically, I'd shape the payload to exactly what this screen displays — a profile summary here probably needs a name and avatar URL, not the full profile object with every settings field, even if the Profile service's native response includes all of that.

I'd version this BFF endpoint explicitly from day one (`/v1/home-feed`), even though it's brand new, because it's cheaper to start with a version in the URL than to retrofit versioning onto an established endpoint later once old clients are already calling it unversioned.

I'd also design each underlying service call to fail somewhat gracefully within the BFF — if Promotions is down, I'd rather return the profile and feed with an empty promotions array than fail the whole screen, since a banner is much less critical than the main feed content.

**Testing:** whether you can design the concrete aggregation, pagination, and payload-shaping choices together for a real screen, not just name the BFF pattern.

interviewQuestions.question: Your team needs to ship a breaking API change — removing a deprecated field that a real percentage of users' old app versions still parse. Walk through how you'd actually roll this out.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First I'd get real data, not a guess: check version-adoption telemetry for exactly what percentage of active users are on app versions that still depend on this field, and whether that percentage is declining fast enough that waiting a few more weeks meaningfully reduces the blast radius, or whether it's plateaued at a stubborn tail that won't naturally disappear.

I would not remove the field from the existing endpoint directly — instead I'd add the change behind a new API version (a new endpoint path or a version header bump), so the old endpoint keeps serving exactly the shape old clients expect, unchanged, indefinitely or until a deliberate sunset. New app builds would call the new versioned endpoint; old installed app versions would keep hitting the old one, since they were built against that contract and can't be retroactively changed.

For the actual sunset of the old version, I'd set a concrete threshold (say, under 1% of active traffic still on the old version) rather than a fixed calendar date disconnected from real adoption, and I'd communicate the eventual cutoff to the team clearly enough that a support playbook exists for the small number of straggler users who do get affected when it finally happens.

The one thing I'd actively avoid is a 'just ship it and see' mutation of the existing shape — for a real user base with a real percentage on old versions, that's not a calculated risk, it's a guaranteed partial outage for a subset of users the moment it deploys.

**Testing:** whether you can execute a genuinely safe breaking-change rollout with real data driving the timeline, not just cite 'version your APIs' as a slogan.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Migration

interviewQuestions.question: Would you build a separate BFF for iOS and a separate one for Android, or one shared mobile BFF for both?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
My default is one shared mobile BFF for iOS and Android, and I'd need a specific reason to split it. iOS and Android's actual data needs for a given screen are usually far more similar to each other than either is to a web dashboard's — both are showing the same screen's content on a phone-sized display with the same bandwidth and battery constraints — so a shared BFF avoids duplicating nearly identical aggregation and shaping logic across two separate services that would drift out of sync over time as each gets maintained somewhat independently.

The case for splitting would be a genuine, sustained divergence in what the two platforms actually need — not a superficial difference like slightly different field naming conventions (which a thin per-platform adapter layer in front of one shared BFF can absorb cheaply), but something structural: one platform needing substantially different aggregation logic because of a platform-specific feature the other doesn't have at all.

If I were advising a team that already has separate iOS and Android BFFs with 90% overlapping logic, I'd flag that as a real duplication cost worth consolidating — every shared business rule that has to be kept in sync across two BFF codebases is a place bugs creep in from drift, not a place genuine platform difference justifies the cost.

**Testing:** whether you default to the lower-duplication option and can articulate what would actually justify the higher-cost alternative, rather than splitting reflexively 'because it's per-platform.'
